measured: The purchase definition covers 4,334 customers, 18,402 purchase invoices, and £8,737,227.64 of merchandise revenue.
The repeat-purchase rate is 65.3%: that is the share of purchasing customers with at least two purchase invoices anywhere in the observed history.
Among customers with at least two purchase invoices, the median average gap between invoices is 54.0 days.
The highest observed purchase-revenue month is 2011-11 at £1,136,534.00. The lowest is 2011-02 at £442,293.59. The latest invoice date is 2011-12-09 12:50:00, so 2011-12 is an incomplete month.
Under the Python RFM rules, the Recent and frequent segment contributes 66.0% of profiled purchase revenue and 25.8% of profiled customers. These segments are rules, not ground-truth labels.

The selected model is random_forest. On the held-out test snapshot its PR-AUC is 0.641, ROC-AUC is 0.742, and F1 at the validation threshold 0.47 is 0.585. Test precision is 0.546 and recall is 0.630.

On the test snapshot, 33.8% of eligible customers purchased again within the horizon. A rule that predicts no purchase for every customer would be right about 66.2% of the time and would have recall 0. The dummy prior model scores every customer at the training base rate. Its F1-maximizing validation threshold is 0.05, which labels every test customer as a purchaser, so its test accuracy equals the positive rate (0.338) and its recall is 1. The selected model's test accuracy was 0.698. That is a modest gap versus the 66.2% majority-class rule, which is why accuracy is a weak way to choose a model when the classes are uneven. Model choice uses validation PR-AUC.
hypotheses: Hypothesis, not a measured outcome: a retention offer aimed at the Inactive segment (1,081 customers, 5.9% of profiled revenue) could be tested with a randomized holdout. The success metric would be the 30-day purchase rate versus the holdout, not the model's historical accuracy.

Hypothesis, not a measured outcome: ranking customers by the model's predicted probability and contacting those below the validation threshold may concentrate outreach. That hypothesis is only supported if a later experiment shows incremental purchases. The score is an association with past repurchase, not a causal effect of intervening.

Hypothesis, not a measured outcome: because one-time and repeat customers can differ in recency and order cadence, a test of reminder timing around the median inter-purchase gap is more informative than a blanket discount. The historical gap is a description of this dataset, not a recommended wait time for another business.
limitations: The source is the UCI Online Retail dataset, a UK gift retailer with many wholesale buyers, from December 2010 through December 2011. It is not AstroTalk customer data and it is not a current consumer-app event stream.
Anonymous invoices are excluded from customer metrics because they have no ID to follow. That removes revenue from the repeat-purchase calculations.
Cancellations and non-merchandise lines are excluded from the purchase definition. A different treatment of returns would change revenue and labels.
The final calendar day is partial. Months and horizons that include it are not a complete day of trade.
RFM segment names are configurable rules. They are not the supervised label and they are not causal clusters.
Model explanations are predictive associations. They do not say that changing recency or spend would cause a purchase.
